description: The Royal African Company, British slave ports, the Somerset case and Black abolitionists.
content_html:
The Atlantic Slave Trade and Britain

The seventeenth and eighteenth centuries saw Britain become the dominant power in the transatlantic slave trade. The Royal African Company was chartered in 1672, establishing Britain’s systematic involvement in the trade in enslaved people. Between 1672 and 1713, the Company transported an estimated 100,000 enslaved Africans across the Middle Passage to the Americas. When its monopoly was broken in 1698, independent merchants from Bristol and Liverpool rapidly expanded the trade. By the mid-eighteenth century, British ships were carrying more enslaved Africans than those of any other nation.

The major British slave-trading ports were London, Bristol and Liverpool. These cities grew wealthy on the profits of the triangular trade — manufactured goods to West Africa, enslaved Africans to the Americas, colonial produce (sugar, tobacco, cotton) back to Britain. This wealth funded the building of churches, country houses, banks and public institutions. Historians including David Olusoga have documented how deeply embedded slave-trade profits were in British urban development and institutional life.

Key Fact

Olaudah Equiano was born around 1745, enslaved and transported to the Americas as a child, and eventually purchased his own freedom. His autobiography, The Interesting Narrative of the Life of Olaudah Equiano (1789), was one of the earliest accounts written by a formerly enslaved person to reach a wide British audience. It sold thousands of copies and was used by abolitionists to demonstrate the humanity and suffering of enslaved Africans. Equiano toured Britain giving lectures and became a leading figure in the campaign against the slave trade.

Black Communities in Eighteenth-Century Britain

The slave trade brought an estimated 10,000–15,000 Black people to Britain by the mid-eighteenth century — largely enslaved servants brought back by planters, merchants and naval officers returning from the colonies. London had the largest Black community, concentrated in areas like St Giles and the East End. Not all were enslaved: some were free, some were formerly enslaved people who had gained freedom, and some were mixed-race children of British colonists.

Ignatius Sancho was born on a slave ship around 1729 and eventually settled in England, where he became a celebrated writer, letter-writer and abolitionist. He was the first Black person known to have voted in a British parliamentary election. His published letters attracted attention from literary figures including Laurence Sterne. Like Equiano, Sancho used his literacy and connections to challenge the dehumanising premises of slavery from within British society.

In 1772, Lord Mansfield delivered a landmark ruling in the Somerset case. James Somerset, an enslaved man brought from the colonies to England, had escaped and been recaptured. His case was taken up by the abolitionist Granville Sharp. Mansfield ruled that Somerset could not be forcibly removed from England. The ruling was widely — but incorrectly — interpreted as making slavery illegal in England. In practice, it only prevented forcible removal; enslaved people could still be held in England, and slavery in the colonies was entirely unaffected.

Nevertheless, the Somerset case had symbolic importance. It galvanised the growing abolitionist movement and gave enslaved people in England a legal foothold. The Sons of Africa, an abolitionist group formed in the 1780s by Equiano and Ottobah Cugoano, drew on the case in their campaigning. The movement connected Black activists with white abolitionists including Thomas Clarkson and William Wilberforce in building the campaign that eventually produced the Slave Trade Act of 1807.

The Zong Massacre and the Path to Abolition

In 1781, the crew of the slave ship Zong threw 132 enslaved Africans overboard alive to claim insurance money, since the company’s policy paid for cargo “lost at sea” but not for those who died of disease. The case came to court in 1783 as an insurance dispute — the legal question was the value of the “cargo,” not the murder of 132 human beings. Granville Sharp tried but failed to bring a murder prosecution. The Zong massacre became one of the most powerful pieces of evidence used by abolitionists to expose the moral horror of the slave trade to British audiences.

The formal abolition of the slave trade in 1807 did not end slavery in the British colonies — that came with the Slavery Abolition Act of 1833. However, the 1807 Act ended Britain’s legal involvement in the trade and was followed by the Royal Navy actively suppressing slave trading by other nations. The compensation paid on abolition in 1833 went to slaveholders, not to the people who had been enslaved — an aspect of the settlement that historians have continued to examine.

Key Fact

The Sons of Africa was founded in the 1780s by Equiano, Ottobah Cugoano and other Black activists. It represents one of the earliest examples of Black political organisation in Britain. The group wrote petitions to Parliament, gave lectures, and worked alongside white abolitionists in what became a broad coalition movement. Their role is sometimes understated in traditional accounts that focus primarily on white parliamentary campaigners.

The growth of Black communities in eighteenth-century Britain fits uneasily within conventional migration narratives because the movement was coerced, not voluntary. Enslaved people did not choose to come to Britain. Yet once in Britain, individuals like Equiano and Sancho demonstrated agency, built networks, and contributed to intellectual and political life in ways that shaped British history. This tension between coerced arrival and active contribution is central to understanding this period of migration history.

The loss of the American colonies after 1783 also contributed to Black community growth in Britain: some Black Loyalists who had fought for the Crown were evacuated to Britain and Canada. This added another layer to a diverse Black British population that came from multiple routes and circumstances, not a single story.
exam_tip_html: When writing about Black communities in eighteenth-century Britain, always distinguish between enslaved people brought to Britain and free Black individuals who were born or who settled here. Use specific named individuals — Equiano, Sancho, Granville Sharp — to anchor your answers. Remember that ‘the Somerset case made slavery illegal’ is a common misconception: it only prevented forcible removal from England and had no effect on slavery in the colonies. For essays on the abolition movement, the Sons of Africa must be included as key agents alongside white campaigners.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Royal African Company (1672) established Britain’s systematic involvement in the transatlantic slave trade; Bristol, Liverpool and London grew wealthy on slave-trade profits, funding buildings and institutions still visible today.
  • Black individuals including Olaudah Equiano and Ignatius Sancho were active agents in British abolition — Equiano’s 1789 autobiography and the Sons of Africa organisation were central to the campaign that produced the Slave Trade Act of 1807.
  • The Somerset case (1772) weakened the legal basis of slavery in England but did not abolish it; formal abolition of slavery in British colonies came in 1833, with compensation going to slaveholders rather than the enslaved.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of Olaudah Equiano's role in the British abolition movement.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark per feature identified, plus 1 mark per supporting detail. Feature 1: Equiano published his autobiography in 1789 (1); it sold thousands of copies and provided first-person evidence of the experience of enslavement that was used by abolitionists to demonstrate the humanity of enslaved Africans (1). Feature 2: Equiano co-founded the Sons of Africa in the 1780s (1); this organisation wrote petitions to Parliament and organised campaigns working alongside white abolitionists such as Clarkson and Wilberforce (1). Maximum 4 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why Black communities grew in Britain during the eighteenth century.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two reasons fully developed. Reason 1: The slave trade brought enslaved Africans to Britain as domestic servants with returning planters, merchants and naval officers; by mid-century, estimates suggest 10,000-15,000 Black people lived in Britain. Reason 2: The loss of the American colonies (1783) led to the evacuation of Black Loyalists who had fought for the Crown to Britain; this added another route of arrival distinct from the slavery system. Secure: Both reasons explained with evidence. Developing: One reason well explained. Emerging: General identification.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the Somerset case of 1772 was significant but limited in its impact on slavery.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Explains what the ruling actually said (Somerset could not be forcibly removed from England) and what it did not say (it did not abolish slavery in England or the colonies); explains significance — it galvanised abolitionists, gave enslaved people a legal foothold, and was widely interpreted as ending slavery in England even though this was inaccurate; notes that slavery in the colonies continued unaffected until 1833. Secure: Explains both the significance and the limitation with evidence. Developing: Notes the importance of the case with some awareness of its limits. Emerging: Basic description.

practice_questions.text: Outline two ways in which profits from the slave trade affected British society and built environment.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 5 marks. Examples: slave-trade wealth funded the building of churches, country houses and public institutions in Bristol and Liverpool (2 marks); the triangular trade made Bristol and Liverpool major cities with global commercial networks (1-2 marks); banks and insurance companies were founded with slave-trade capital (1 mark). Maximum 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: How far do you agree that Black activists were more important than white campaigners in the abolition of the slave trade? Use your knowledge and any interpretations you have studied.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Sustained argument weighing the contributions of the Sons of Africa (Equiano, Cugoano — petitions, public lectures, Equiano's autobiography) against white abolitionists (Clarkson's empirical research, Wilberforce's parliamentary campaigning, Sharp's legal work); recognises the coalition nature of the movement and the historical tendency to understate Black agency; considers that without Black testimony, the abolitionist case would have been weaker. Secure: Clear argument with evidence from both sides. Developing: Some comparison with basic evidence. Emerging: Descriptive. SPaG: 5 marks.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the growth of the slave trade changed Black communities in Britain between 1672 and 1807.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering: Two changes explained with causal analysis. Change 1: A free Black community developed alongside enslaved residents — as individual cases like Somerset's produced partial legal protections, formerly enslaved people gained freedom and formed networks that contributed to public and intellectual life. Change 2: Political organisation emerged — from isolated individuals like Sancho in the 1760s to the organised Sons of Africa in the 1780s, Black activists developed collective campaigning capacity. Secure: Two changes with relevant evidence. Developing: One change explained. Emerging: General statements.

knowledge_checks.q: In what year was Olaudah Equiano's autobiography published?
What did Lord Mansfield's ruling in the Somerset case (1772) actually decide?
options: That slavery was illegal throughout Britain and its colonies
That enslaved people could not be forcibly removed from England against their will
That the slave trade must be abolished within five years
That compensation must be paid to formerly enslaved people

knowledge_checks.q: The Royal African Company, chartered in _____, transported an estimated 100,000 enslaved Africans before its monopoly was broken in 1698.
The _____ was an abolitionist group founded in the 1780s by Equiano and Ottobah Cugoano, writing petitions to Parliament and campaigning against the slave trade.
Match each individual to their significance in eighteenth-century Black British history.
right: Formerly enslaved author whose 1789 autobiography drove abolitionist campaigning
Writer and composer, first Black person known to vote in a British election
White abolitionist lawyer who pursued the Somerset case and Zong massacre

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Royal African Company chartered?

flashcard_questions.a: Formerly enslaved African whose 1789 autobiography became central to the British abolition movement
Black British writer and abolitionist (c.1729-1780), first Black person known to vote in a British election
Crew threw 132 enslaved Africans overboard to claim insurance — became key evidence for abolitionists

flashcard_questions.q: What did the Somerset case (1772) rule?
flashcard_questions.a: Enslaved person James Somerset could not be forcibly removed from England against his will

flashcard_questions.q: What was the Sons of Africa?
flashcard_questions.a: Abolitionist group founded in the 1780s by Equiano and Cugoano — one of Britain's earliest Black political organisations

flashcard_questions.q: When was the Slave Trade Act passed?
flashcard_questions.a: 1807 — abolished Britain's legal involvement in the slave trade

flashcard_questions.q: When was slavery abolished in British colonies?
flashcard_questions.a: 1833, by the Slavery Abolition Act — compensation went to slaveholders, not the enslaved

flashcard_questions.q: Which English city became the largest slave-trading port by the mid-eighteenth century?
flashcard_questions.a: Liverpool (alongside Bristol and London, which also grew wealthy on the trade)

glossary_terms.definition: A royal monopoly company chartered in 1672 to conduct the slave trade between West Africa and the English colonies; it transported an estimated 100,000 enslaved Africans before its monopoly was broken in 1698.

Formerly enslaved African writer, born around 1745, whose autobiography published in 1789 became a key text in the British abolition movement and documented the experience of the Middle Passage and slavery.
Writer, composer and abolitionist (c.1729-1780), born on a slave ship and later settled in England, one of the earliest Black British authors and a prominent voice against slavery.

A 1772 legal case in which Lord Mansfield ruled that an enslaved person, James Somerset, could not be forcibly removed from England against his will, significantly weakening the legal basis of slavery in England.

An abolitionist group founded in the 1780s by Olaudah Equiano, Ottobah Cugoano and other Black activists in Britain, who wrote petitions, gave speeches and organised campaigns against the slave trade.
